questions.q: What are the three key differences between optimizing a quantum cost function and optimizing a typical classical ML loss function, according to the lesson?
options: Quantum evaluations are slow (queueing), expensive (real money per shot), and noisy (statistical estimates from finite shots) -- unlike cheap, instant, exact classical evaluations
Quantum cost functions have no gradients at all, so only gradient-free methods can ever be used
Quantum evaluations are faster, cheaper, and more exact than classical ones
There is no real difference; any classical ML optimizer works identically in both settings
questions.explain: The lesson identifies slowness (queueing), real monetary cost per shot, and shot noise as the three properties that rule out or deprioritize optimizer choices that assume cheap, instant, exact evaluations.

questions.q: For a 20-parameter circuit, how many circuit evaluations does ONE iteration of the parameter-shift rule require, versus one iteration of SPSA?
options: Parameter-shift: 41 (2x20+1); SPSA: 2, regardless of parameter count
Parameter-shift: 2; SPSA: 41
Both require exactly 20 evaluations per iteration
Parameter-shift: 20; SPSA: 20
questions.explain: Parameter-shift needs 2 evaluations per parameter plus 1 for the cost itself (2x20+1=41). SPSA always needs only 2 evaluations per iteration, since it perturbs all parameters simultaneously in one random direction.

questions.q: In the worked 100-iteration comparison on a 20-parameter circuit, what was the approximate cost ratio between parameter-shift and SPSA at 1,000 shots/eval on Rigetti Ankaa-3 pricing?
options: Parameter-shift cost about 20x more ($4,920 vs $240)
SPSA cost about 20x more than parameter-shift
Both cost exactly the same amount
Parameter-shift was free; only SPSA incurred cost
questions.explain: Parameter-shift's 4,100 total evaluations cost $4,920, while SPSA's 200 total evaluations cost $240 -- roughly a 20x difference, driven by parameter-shift's per-parameter evaluation scaling.

questions.q: The lesson notes that even if SPSA needs 3x more iterations than parameter-shift to reach comparable accuracy on the 20-parameter example, SPSA ($720) still beats parameter-shift ($4,920). What general principle does this illustrate?
options: There is a crossover point where a gradient-free method's much lower per-iteration cost outweighs needing more iterations, which is why gradient-free methods dominate for circuits with more than a handful of parameters
SPSA is always cheaper than parameter-shift regardless of parameter count or iteration multiplier
Iteration count has no effect on total cost in hybrid optimization
Parameter-shift is never a reasonable choice for any circuit
questions.explain: The crossover point depends on parameter count and how many extra iterations the noisier gradient-free method needs -- but for circuits with enough parameters, the per-iteration savings dominate even after accounting for needing more iterations.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend setting an optimizer's convergence tolerance relative to the expected shot-noise standard error, rather than an arbitrarily small number?
options: A tolerance tighter than the shot-noise floor causes the loop to keep running, chasing improvements that are actually just statistical noise and will never resolve, wasting QPU budget
Tolerance has no relationship to shot noise; it should always be set to zero
A looser tolerance always produces a more accurate final answer
Shot noise only matters for amplitude encoding, not for optimizer configuration
questions.explain: Since each cost evaluation carries shot-noise uncertainty, a tolerance set tighter than that noise floor causes the optimizer to keep iterating in pursuit of 'improvements' that are really just measurement fluctuations -- burning budget without converging to a better true answer.
